title: Spectral Gaps with Quantum Counting Queries and Oblivious State Preparation
abstract: Approximating the k -th spectral gap Δ k = | λ k − λ k + 1 | and the corresponding midpoint μ k = λ k + λ k + 1 2 of an N × N Hermitian matrix with eigenvalues λ 1 ≥ λ 2 ≥ … ≥ λ N , is an important special case of the eigenproblem with numerous applications in science and engineering. In this work, we present a quantum algorithm which approximates these values up to additive error ϵ Δ k using a logarithmic number of qubits. Notably, in the QRAM model, its total complexity (queries and gates) is bounded by O ( N 2 ϵ 2 Δ k 2 p o l y l o g ( N , 1 Δ k , 1 ϵ , 1 δ ) ) , where ϵ , δ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) are the accuracy and the failure probability, respectively. For large gaps Δ k , this provides a speed-up against the best-known complexities of classical algorithms, namely, O ( N ω p o l y l o g ( N , 1 Δ k , 1 ϵ ) ) , where ω ≲ 2.371 is the matrix multiplication exponent. A key technical step in the analysis is the preparation of a suitable random initial state, which ultimately allows us to efficiently count the number of eigenvalues that are smaller than a threshold, while maintaining a quadratic complexity in N . In the black-box access model, we also report an Ω ( N 2 ) query lower bound for deciding the existence of a spectral gap in a binary (albeit non-symmetric) matrix.

    Problem 1.1 has numerous applications in different areas. In numerical analysis, esti-
mating spectral gaps is a key subroutine of so-called spectral divide-and-conquer algorithms
for diagonalizing matrices [1, 2, 3, 4]. These methods rely on finding a “splitting” point
µ that does not coincide with an eigenvalue; our midpoint estimator µk = (λk + λk+1 )/2
provides a natural and well-conditioned choice for such a split, as it maximizes the distance
to the nearest eigenvalues. In data analytics, a large gap in the spectrum of a data matrix
indicates a separation between the actual information and the “noise” in the data. This
phenomenon is often used in Principal Component Analysis [5, 6] to identify good splitting
points, or “elbows”, for dimensionality reduction, data visualization, and noise filtering. By
directly targeting the k-th gap, our algorithm enables the automated detection of these
elbows without requiring the explicit computation of (potentially large) subsets of singular
values or a full singular value decomposition (SVD). In spectral graph theory, gaps be-
tween the eigenvalues of the graph Laplacian reveal connectivity properties, and they can
be used, for example, to identify communities, [7, 8, 9, 10].
    In the study of quantum phase transitions, the closing of the k-th gap, where λk+1 −
λk → 0 as the system size increases, serves as a key indicator of topological or magnetic
phase transitions [11]. In the context of quantum computing, the size of the spectral gap
also determines the runtime of adiabatic state preparation, since the adiabatic theorem
requires the evolution time to scale inversely with (a power of) the minimum spectral
gap encountered [12]. Last but not least, spectral gaps are also important in electronic
structure calculations, for example, to estimate the energy gap (Fermi level) that separates
the occupied and unoccupied states of the underlying system [13, 14, 15, 16]. In that
direction, our gap estimator could be combined with the techniques of [17] to calculate the
electron density of a system at zero temperature.
    The aim of this work is to provide a detailed analysis of quantum algorithms for solving
Problem 1.1, aiming for provable approximation guarantees and end-to-end worst-case
complexity bounds.

1.1 Existing algorithms and complexity bounds
Here we give a brief overview of the related algorithms literature. We first recall that, from
the Abel-Ruffini theorem, computing eigenvalues of general matrices is intractable in the

it consists of two phases:

safely count eigenvalues. If not, we keep searching for smaller gaps. This way we have full
control of the value of ∆, and, consequently, of the cost of eigenvalue counting.

4 Complexity in QRAM
In this section we specialize the complexity analysis in the QRAM model [58]. We describe
a specific technique to construct block-encodings via the so-called quantum-accessible data
structures, studied in [41, 49, 50, 65]. We assume a dense N × N matrix A ∈ C, whose
elements are known (i.e. pre-computed), and stored as an array in a classical memory.
Given this classical array, a data structure of the form of [41] can be constructed in an
offline fashion and stored in a classical memory in O(N 2 ) arithmetic operations, and it
requires O(N 2 log(N )) space, i.e. words, assuming each matrix element requires one word
to store.
     For dense matrices, the data structure consists of N binary trees with O(log(N )) depth
and N leaves each. If we were to prepare a quantum circuit for the access oracle of this
data structure, we would need O(N 2 ) gates to implement it. To elaborate more, each

be constructed using O(N ) one and two qubit gates (rotations and CNOT gates) [66, 67],
and we need such a circuit for every i ∈ [N ]. However, if the quantum computer has
the ability to query the elements of the classical data structure in superposition, which is
possible in the QRAM model, the gate complexity can be reduced to O(polylog(N )) [41].

5 A lower bound in the Black-Box model
In this section we derive a lower bound for the problem of deciding the existence of a
spectral gap of a binary matrix, in the so-called Black-Box access model. Here we assume
a unitary OA through which we can query elements of the matrix A via:

                                   OA : |i⟩ |j⟩ |0⟩ 7→ |i⟩ |j⟩ |Ai,j ⟩ .

Several lower bounds are known for related problems. A straightforward query lower bound
for determining the midpoint µk can be obtained from the median problem [68]. Let A
be a quantum algorithm which, given OA , and an integer k, it returns any (classical)
value µek such that µ ek ∈ (λk , λk+1 ). Then A can be directly used to solve the median
problem, where, given oracle access to a sequence of N numbers {x1 , . . . , xN }, where N
is even, we seek to find a number that lies strictly inside x ∈ (xN/2 , xN/2 + 1). Such a
sequence can be seen as the elements of a diagonal matrix, and the eigenvalues of such a
matrix are the diagonal elements themselves. [68] proved a Ω(N ) query lower bound for the
median problem, assuming that we have oracle access to a quantum circuit implementing
the sequence. Indeed, the same bound holds even if we only want to verify that µ ek is inside
the correct interval, since this generalizes the counting problem [68, 69, 70].
    Here we obtain a stronger lower bound for deciding whether there exists a gap be-
tween two consecutive eigenvalues, inspired by the reductions of [56, 57]. We remark that
the construction below is inherently non-Hermitian. Whether analogous black-box lower
bounds hold for Hermitian matrices remains an open question.

6 Conclusion
In this work we studied algorithms for computing spectral gaps between eigenvalues of
Hermitian matrices and the corresponding midpoints. One of the main subroutines is a
randomized state preparation method, which achieves at least 1/N overlap with any fixed
target state with probability at least 3/5, and requires O(N ) classical random bits to
prepare. This can be used to efficiently approximate the smallest singular value of a block-
encoded matrix with high probability, and to count the eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix
that are smaller than a given threshold. In the quantum-accessible data structure model,
the total query complexity of our main algorithm scales at most quadratically with respect
to the problem size N . This indicates the potential for a polynomial quantum speed-
up, since the complexity of the best-known classical algorithms require O(N

operations. In the black-box access model, we also proved an Ω(N ) query lower bound for

A Preliminaries on block-encodings and eigenvalue transformation
In this section we recall some basic definitions and known results for block-encodings.
Block-encoding refers to the derivation of a unitary operator UA which can be described
by a quantum circuit and “encodes” a given matrix A, which was stated in Definition 1.1.
    Constructing block-encodings with low cost is not a trivial task. A common approach in
the literature is to assume a “black-box” unitary oracle that gives access to a (sparse) matrix
A. See eg. [49, 71]. Recent works take a step further, describing explicit quantum circuits
for the block-encoding of special classes of matrices [72, 73, 50, 74]. In the main algorithm
we assume the existence of a general subroutine that can prepare block-encodings, defined
as follows.

and an accuracy ϵ, and prepares an (a, b, ϵ)-QUBE of A. a and b might be functions of N
or ∥A∥ξ , for some norm ξ.
